In SCOPe 2.08 (the current release; latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16), histones are in Class a (all-alpha proteins), Fold a.22 (Histone-fold, sunid 47112), Superfamily a.22.1 (Histone-fold, sunid 47113). The proteins related to histones sit in the same superfamily, and they are split into families below it:

- a.22.1.1, Nucleosome core histones (sunid 47114). These are the eukaryotic histones themselves: H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, plus macro-H2A.1 histone domain and automated matches. This is the closest relationship, the same family as the canonical histones.
- a.22.1.2, Archaeal histone (sunid 47129), for example Methanothermus fervidus histones A and B (protein sunid 68897, species sunids 68895 and 68896). These are the prokaryotic homologues of the eukaryotic core histones. They are in the same superfamily but a different family: homology is supported, but sequence identity is low or functional and structural divergence is large enough that SCOPe does not call them the same family.
- a.22.1.3, TBP-associated factors, TAFs (sunid 47134). This family holds histone-fold domains of the transcription machinery: TAF(II)18, 28, 42, 62, TAF4 (hTAF(II)135) and TAF12, and also NC2 alpha and beta (negative cofactor 2), NF-Y subunits (NF-YB and NF-YC), and the chromatin remodeller subunits Chrac-14 and Chrac-16. It also holds an odd member, the histone domain of Son of sevenless (SOS). These are paralogue-like histone-fold proteins that mostly heterodimerise through the histone fold, as H3/H4 and H2A/H2B do. They are related by a shared histone fold, not by being histones.
- a.22.1.4, Bacterial histone-fold protein (sunid 101318), with hypothetical proteins Aq_328 (Aquifex) and TTHA1479 (Thermus). This family is a bacterial member of the superfamily. Nothing is known about its function, so it should not be assumed to bind DNA or package chromatin like histones.
- a.22.1.0, automated matches (sunid 238448). This is a bookkeeping grouping, not a biological family.

So, in SCOPe terms: class a, fold a.22 and superfamily a.22.1 are shared by all of these proteins, and the family level separates them. SCOPe puts the shared superfamily at the level of probable common evolutionary origin, supported by structure and function. The fold has only one superfamily here, so fold and superfamily coincide in membership.

Limits: Superfamily membership means a probable common ancestor and a shared histone-fold core (a long central helix flanked by two shorter helices, in a handshake-type dimer). It does not mean the same function, the same DNA or nucleosome binding, or a single ortholog relationship. TAFs, NC2, NF-Y, CHRAC and SOS histone-fold domains do different jobs from nucleosome core histones. The family or protein level is the right level for transferring any function, and only a.22.1.1 members are canonical nucleosome histones. Other histone-related proteins that are not in a.22 are separate in SCOPe. Examples are linker histone H1 or H5 and Hho1p, which are winged-helix proteins (a.4.5.13, a different fold), and histone-modifying enzymes such as HDAC8 (c.42.1.2) or Dot1l (c.66.1.31). The names match, but there is no structural or evolutionary relationship to the histone fold. I did not verify the full set of members beyond the children listings I retrieved.
